question: Can a coding agent improve the learning algorithm in an existing research repository, rather than merely tune hyperparameters or execution, under a clean-start and hidden-final-evaluation protocol?

key_findings.claim: Current agents make little absolute progress on algorithm design in this benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: Across 29 configurations of six systems and ten tasks, the mean normalized score is 0.166 and the best system mean is 0.250, where the shipped algorithm is 0.1 and the task optimum is 1.0; 124 of 290 cells score below the shipped baseline.

key_findings.claim: Most completed submissions change how a run is executed, not how the model learns.
key_findings.evidence: Of 263 classifiable changed submissions, 141 (53.6%) only alter run-side factors and 122 (46.4%) touch a learning family. The latter average 0.226 versus 0.126 for run-side-only submissions, although this is observational rather than a randomized treatment effect.

anchors.section: 4.1 Most submissions change how the run goes, not how the model learns

key_findings.claim: Higher reasoning effort mainly increases willingness to attempt algorithmic changes, completion, and experiment count, but does not move systems near the optimum.
key_findings.evidence: The learning-side share rises from 8% at the lowest effort to 64% at the highest, while mean score rises from 0.094 to 0.196. In the Codex grid, median evaluations increase from 4 to 16 and edited lines from 18 to 246, but the highest-effort mean remains only 0.196.

anchors.section: 4.2 Reasoning effort buys nerve, and nerve is what pays

key_findings.claim: The strongest qualitative successes start by building a diagnostic or faster measurement instrument before changing the method.
key_findings.evidence: The paper traces three successful cases to a solver that exposes a task ceiling, a weight-soup evaluator accelerated from roughly 190 seconds to 0.38 seconds, and localization of an in-place activation-overwrite bug before revising one-shot pruning.

anchors.section: 4.3 What the submissions that reached the algorithmic layer did
4.3 What the submissions that reached the algorithmic layer did

method.core_idea: Freeze ten real research repositories from different training-algorithm families, let agents modify their source under a fixed exploration budget, then rerun only the resulting source from a clean start and score it with a final evaluator unavailable during development.
method.mechanism: Each task exposes a cheap proxy for four hours on one B300, accepts a source patch rather than weights or cache, and runs that patch for up to twelve hours. A task-specific monotone transform maps an uninformative model to 0, the shipped method to 0.1, and the task optimum to 1.0. A separate model classifies diffs into four run-side and four learning-side change families.
assumptions: The ten repositories represent algorithmic-design capability beyond their specific tasks and compute regime.
The hidden final evaluator and clean-start replay prevent direct final-metric overfitting and inheritance of exploration artifacts.
The chosen uninformative point, optimum, and monotone coordinate make cross-task score averaging meaningful.
A language-model classifier can reliably distinguish run-side edits from changes to objectives, supervision, update rules, or data.

techniques.role: Separates freely queried development proxies from the metric that determines the final score.
Reapplies source changes in a fresh environment so exploration weights, rollouts, and caches cannot leak into verification.
Maps incommensurable metrics to a shared progress coordinate anchored at an uninformative model, the shipped baseline, and an explicit optimum.
Labels patches by the mechanism they alter, allowing outcome gains to be separated from evidence of algorithm invention.

evaluations.setting: 29 model-harness-effort configurations from six systems on ten algorithm-family tasks, 290 cells total
evaluations.metric: Mean task-normalized score, with shipped algorithm at 0.1 and optimum at 1.0
evaluations.result: Study mean 0.166; best system Claude Opus 5 at 0.250; best single configuration Claude Opus 5 medium at 0.288; 124 of 290 cells fall below 0.1
evaluations.baseline: Each repository's unmodified source, rerun with the same hardware, budget, evaluator, and evaluation asset

evaluations.setting: 263 submissions with at least one classifiable change
evaluations.metric: Normalized score grouped by whether any learning-side family is changed
evaluations.result: 122 learning-side submissions average 0.226; 141 run-side-only submissions average 0.126; reported gap 0.100 with standard error 0.022
evaluations.baseline: Run-side-only submissions; the comparison is correlational because stronger systems also reach the learning side more often

evaluations.metric: Learning-side change share and mean normalized score
evaluations.result: Learning-side share rises from 8% to 64%, and mean score rises from 0.094 to 0.196; within the Codex grid the score rises from 0.094 to 0.204

limitations: The authors state that the benchmark compares agents with repository baselines, not human experts, so it does not locate human-level algorithm-design performance.
The authors state that some proxy and final evaluations draw from the same corpus; the protocol blocks access to the final metric, but does not always guarantee sample-disjoint development data.
The authors note that the learning-side score gap is observational: systems that make algorithmic edits more often may already be stronger.
Reviewer inference: ten repositories, one B300 exploration regime, and one clean-start run per cell provide limited evidence about robustness across seeds, larger budgets, or other research domains.
Reviewer inference: averaging task-normalized scores depends materially on hand-chosen uninformative and optimum anchors, especially where a mathematical optimum is not practically attainable.
failure_modes: An agent can optimize the development proxy in a way that does not transfer to the inaccessible final evaluator.
A patch can pass startup checks but yield no loadable merged model or violate an artifact gate after the twelve-hour replay.
A large engineering refactor can be mistaken for algorithm invention, or a compact learning-rule change can be missed, if the diff classifier is unreliable.
A best-of-three-checkpoint policy can favor noisy checkpoints, especially when final evaluation itself has sampling variance.
A method may exploit idiosyncrasies of one frozen repository without representing a reusable or scalable learning algorithm.
reusable_insights: Evaluate automated research with a source-only handoff and clean replay; carrying exploratory artifacts forward confounds method quality with search expenditure.
Measure what an agent changed, not only the resulting score, whenever the target capability is method invention rather than unrestricted artifact improvement.
Give every environment explicit uninformative, baseline, and target anchors before aggregating heterogeneous rewards.
Treat fast, trustworthy instrumentation as a first-class search action: strong method changes often follow a measurable diagnosis rather than undirected patch generation.
Separate proxy validity, artifact validity, and final improvement into distinct gates so reward hacking and engineering failure remain visible.
open_questions: How stable are the system rankings and learning-side effects across independent exploration and replay seeds?
Can a patch-level ontology be validated against blinded human expert labels and causal ablations of the edited mechanisms?
Which proxy-to-final relationships best predict genuine algorithm transfer rather than benchmark-specific improvement?
Do methods discovered on small models and twelve-hour budgets preserve their ordering when model size, data, and training horizon scale?
Can an agent trained on this benchmark improve its diagnostic behavior without learning evaluator-specific shortcuts?

competitive_landscape.title: MLS-Bench: A Holistic and Rigorous Assessment of AI Systems on Building Better AI
competitive_landscape.difference: MLS-Bench tests 140 targeted components and explicitly asks whether improvements generalize and scale; AI4AI-Bench instead freezes ten full repositories, isolates learning-algorithm edits from execution changes, and performs hidden clean-start replay.

competitive_landscape.title: Agent^2 RL-Bench: Can LLM Agents Engineer Agentic RL Post-Training?
competitive_landscape.difference: Agent^2 RL-Bench focuses on six post-training tasks and whether agents can close static-to-online RL pipelines; AI4AI-Bench covers ten algorithm families and audits whether any gain came from the learning procedure rather than the broader pipeline.

competitive_landscape.title: MLR-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on Open-Ended Machine Learning Research
competitive_landscape.difference: MLR-Bench evaluates end-to-end research artifacts on 201 workshop tasks with an LLM judge and highlights fabricated experiments; AI4AI-Bench narrows the claim to executable algorithm changes with repository baselines and fixed evaluators.

competitive_landscape.title: PostTrainBench: Can LLM Agents Automate LLM Post-Training?
competitive_landscape.difference: PostTrainBench grants broad autonomy over data, web use, and post-training strategy and documents evaluator abuse; AI4AI-Bench constrains source handoff and final evaluation to isolate algorithmic changes across more learning families.

novelty_assessment: The authors claim the first benchmark that makes the algorithmic-design step itself the object of evaluation. Reviewer inference: the strongest novelty is the combination of source-only clean replay, hidden final evaluation, repository-matched baselines, cross-task normalization, and a patch-mechanism ontology. Neighboring benchmarks already test autonomous ML research and post-training, so the novelty is isolation and attribution rather than the general idea of benchmarking AI research agents.
reviewer_notes: Read all 19 extracted pages, including the task definitions and complete example contract. Quantitative results are author-reported. Causal interpretations and scale-transfer concerns are explicitly marked as reviewer inference.
